title: integration-effort-sla-negotiation-guide-llm-apis
content:
Purpose:
This is a working brief for GTM + sales engineering that frames argued positions and negotiation scripts when we compete against other LLM API providers. Focus: quantify and de-risk integration effort and SLA tradeoffs — a unique angle that surfaces hidden costs for buyers.

Audience:
- Sales reps and solutions engineers engaging mid-market and enterprise prospects evaluating inference endpoints.
- RevOps/sales leadership preparing negotiation playbooks and contract anchors.

Top-line messaging pillars (short):
1) Integration cost is the largest multi-month friction — we win when we demonstrate predictable, low-effort integration paths and testable performance.
2) SLAs are not just uptime numbers — they imply observability, traceability, and firm recovery playbooks.
3) Operational compatibility (retries, streaming, batching semantics, KV-cache sharing) determines total cost-of-ownership more than headline token price.

Quick positioning vs generic LLM API competitors:
- Claim: "Lower integration lift and clearer SLAs reduce hidden migration costs."
- Proof points: well-documented SDKs (Python/TS), first-request tracing, tenant-level performance profiles, explicit rollback and model-variant fallbacks built into the platform.
- Vulnerabilities: Customers familiar with a single-vendor API will cite simpler initial setup; emphasize long-term predictability and SRE playbook.

Integration-effort map (talking points to quantify in conversations):
- Onboarding dev time estimate (typical):
  - 2–4 dev-days for a single-route PoC with our SDK + streaming enabled
  - 1–2 dev-weeks to wire up production-grade batching, retry/backoff, prefix caching and telemetry
- Typical blocker sources: authentication KMS/KV integration, VPC peering for Private, payload schema (tool-calling) mismatch, streaming interop, and request/response size limits.
- Competitive comparison checklist (call out vs competitor):
  - SDK parity: do they support typed SDKs, backpressure controls, and streaming client libs?
  - Dev tooling: local emulator, end-to-end test harness, perf testing artifacts
  - Telemetry: token-level cost traces, per-request latency breakdowns, cold-start metrics
  - Migration aids: model-variant mapping, pin-by-versioning, canary rollouts and automatic fallback

SLA negotiation playbook (phrases and anchors):
- Frame: "We typically compress uptime, latency, and time-to-recovery into a single operational promise backed by runbooks."
- Example asks to include in term sheet (starter list):
  - Availability target: 99.95% for production endpoints (region-scoped)
  - P99 latency SLO: define baseline per model-class (e.g., 200ms for small chat models, 800ms for long-context models) measured at edge egress with 95th percentile per 30-day window
  - Incident RTO: customer-facing mitigation (automatic fallbacks) within 5 minutes; full restoration RTO 2 hours for severity-1
  - Credit regime: pro-rated credits based on sustained SLA breach (define measurement methodology)
  - Observability: access to request-level traces and token-cost invoicing for last 90 days
- Negotiation anchors: start with higher SLAs for committed-reserved capacity and tiered response SLAs for bursts. Trade credits for committed spend rather than unlimited penalty exposure.

Operational asks — what to require during contracting:
- Test hooks: a test endpoint that mirrors production latency for a limited time window for baseline verification
- Data isolation and retention: explicit audit-log retention window and per-request redaction controls
- Support: 24/7 escalation contacts for severity-1 incidents for enterprise contracts; defined SLA for initial response (15 minutes)
- Runbook access: redacted incident runbooks + postmortem within agreed cadence (72 hours after incident close)

Objection handling snippets (for SEs to use verbatim):
- "Your token price is lower, why shouldn't I go with them?"
  - Response: "Price is only part of the equation — our customers typically see a hidden 2–6x cost multiplier from integration, telemetry gaps, and fallback engineering when the unexpected happens. We accelerate your path to stable ops with baked-in fallbacks, model pinning, and per-token observability."
- "We already have a vendor; migration is risky."
  - Response: "We reduce migration risk by offering traffic shadowing, per-route canaries, and model-variant compatibility layers so you can stage traffic gradually and validate quality and latency without user-facing impact."
- "We care most about latency — how do you compare?"
  - Response: "We publish P50/P90/P99 profiles per region and per model class. For our small-medium chat profiles we routinely hit X% faster P99 than peers due to runtime optimizations and continuous batching; if latency is critical we can run a joint perf test in your environment."

Negotiation tactics and concession levers (ranked by cost to us):
1) Reserved capacity commit (high value): give stronger latency SLAs and dedicated routing for medium/large commits.
2) Observability access (low cost): provide request-level traces for enterprise customers in contract.
3) Credits vs. monetary penalties (low-medium cost): prefer credits or service credits rather than cash penalties to align incentives and cap exposure.
4) Pricing floors for model variants (medium cost): lock a price for a defined model family for N months with volume tiers.

Integration checklist for SEs (use during PoC and discovery):
- Auth: KMS, API key rotation, service-accounts (list existing encumbrances)
- Networking: VPC peering, egress policies, bandwidth constraints
- Data: PII redaction, retention policy, KMS/HSM integration, transfer logs
- Telemetry: example logs (request-id, model-id, tokens-in/out, latency breakdowns)
- Resilience: fallback routes (smaller/quantized variants), rate-limits, circuit-breakers test plan
- Compliance: SOC2 controls mapping, encryption-in-transit + at-rest, audit log retention

Sample SE conversation checklist (short bullets to keep on calls):
- Ask: "What does your current observability show for per-request latency and token cost?"
- Ask: "Do you require on-prem/private deployment or is VPC adequate?"
- Ask: "Describe your worst-case traffic spike — how many concurrent requests and what tail latency are you targeting?"
- Validate: "Do you already have a batching or caching layer in front of LLM calls?"

Common traps to call out to customers (we use to highlight competitor risk):
- Token-only comparisons: vendor prints per-token price but omits average tokens-per-invocation and extra egress charges.
- Ambiguous measurement windows: vendors use different measurement points (edge vs origin) — ask for exact measurement locations and methods.
- Missing forensic telemetry: no per-request token breakdown or request-level traces => expensive bug hunts.
- Implicit vendor lock with proprietary SDKs and opaque model-variant mappings.

Playbook snippets for legal & procurement (talking points for commercial team):
- Ask for explicit measurement methodology, sample test harness that both parties run, and joint acceptance criteria for performance.
- Prefer credits over cash penalties; if cash penalties are required, cap at a fixed percentage of committed monthly spend.
- Ensure audit access: at least read-only for request-level logs for 90 days and aggregated metrics for 3 years.

Appendix: quick perf test template (what to run during PoC)
- Generate synthetic workload matching target distribution: 70% short-chat (<=128 tokens), 20% medium (128–512), 10% long (>=512).
- Run for 1 hour at target concurrency (e.g., 200 qps) and collect P50/P90/P99 tail latencies and token throughput.
- Capture cold-start behavior by cycling 5–10 minute idle periods and measuring first-request latency.

Open questions / TODOs (internal):
- Create a one-click perf-script in our public SDK repo that SEs can run against customer test keys (linked PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/312).
- Formalize pricing concession matrix for reserved capacity vs. SLA strength (owner: Maya).
- Align legal with required telemetry access language for enterprise agreements (owner: Ethan).

Notes to self (SE tactics):
- Always trade an SLA ask for a committed spend; quantify the delta in example numbers during the call.
- Use a live perf test early with a shadowed route to build credibility — customers trust data.
- Keep a short checklist for legal so procurement requests are quick and consistent.

End of brief.
